section.title: Submit to Authority and God's Ways
section.sectionRationale: The Teacher turns from private wisdom to life lived under power we do not control: kings whose word is final, a world where the wicked are honored and the righteous get what the wicked deserve. He counsels wise navigation under authority, then presses past every visible injustice to a conviction he cannot prove but will not surrender, that in the end it will go well with those who fear God.
section.thesis: Wisdom teaches us to live shrewdly under authority we cannot command and in a world we cannot decode; yet beneath the surface tangle of injustice the Teacher holds fast that it will go well with those who fear God, even though no one under the sun can fathom what God is doing.
section.frameNote: Three movements: keeping the king's command with the timing and discernment of wisdom; the anchor of the passage, that it will go well with those who fear God though the sinner seems to prosper; and the confession that God's ways are futile to trace out, beyond the reach of even the wise.

verses.text: Who is like the wise man? Who knows the interpretation of a matter? A man’s {{chokmah|wisdom}} brightens his face, and the sternness of his face is changed.
Keep the king’s command, I say, because of your oath before God.
Do not hasten to leave his presence, and do not persist in a bad cause, for he will do whatever he pleases.
For the king’s word is supreme, and who can say to him, “What are you doing?”
Whoever keeps his command will come to no harm, and a wise heart knows the right time and procedure.
For there is a right time and procedure to every purpose, though a man’s misery weighs heavily upon him.
Since no one knows what will happen, who can tell him what is to come?
As no man has power over the wind to contain it, so no one has authority over his day of death. As no one can be discharged in wartime, so wickedness will not release those who practice it.
All this I have seen, applying my mind to every deed that is done under the sun; there is a time when one man lords it over another to his own detriment.

units.label: It will go well with those who fear God

verses.text: Then too, I saw the burial of the wicked who used to go in and out of the holy place, and they were praised in the city where they had done so. This too is {{hevel|futile}}.
When the sentence for a crime is not speedily executed, the hearts of men become fully set on doing evil.
Although a sinner does evil a hundred times and still lives long, yet I also know that it will go well with those who fear God, who are reverent in His presence.
Yet because the wicked do not fear God, it will not go well with them, and their days will not lengthen like a shadow.

units.label: God's ways are mysterious
units.note: futility, joy, and the limit of wisdom

verses.text: There is a {{hevel|futility}} that is done on the earth: There are righteous men who get what the actions of the wicked deserve, and there are wicked men who get what the actions of the righteous deserve. I say that this too is futile.

So I commended the enjoyment of life, because there is nothing better for a man under the sun than to eat and drink and be merry. For this joy will accompany him in his labor during the days of his life that God gives him under the sun.
When I applied my mind to know wisdom and to observe the task that one performs on the earth, though his eyes do not see sleep in the day or even in the night,

I saw every work of God, and that a man is unable to comprehend the work that is done under the sun. Despite his efforts to search it out, he cannot find its meaning; even if the wise man claims to know, he is unable to comprehend.

chokmah.gloss: Wisdom, skill for living well. In Ecclesiastes it is real and valuable, brightening a face and teaching the right time and procedure, yet the Teacher insists it cannot finally master death or decode all that God is doing under the sun.

hevel.gloss: Literally a breath or vapor, the keyword of the book, often rendered vanity, futility, or fleeting. It names what cannot be grasped or held: here the honoring of the wicked and the reversal of just deserts, a haze that hangs over life under the sun until God Himself resolves it.

basic.context: After chapters of testing pleasure, work, and wisdom, the Teacher looks at life under power he cannot control. He counsels his readers to keep the king's command and to act with the discernment of wisdom, knowing the right time and manner for things, because a ruler's word is final and no one holds authority over his own day of death. Then he names the thing that troubles him most: the wicked are buried with honor, sentences go unexecuted, and often the righteous get what the wicked deserve while the wicked get what the righteous deserve. He calls this futile. Yet in the middle of it he plants a conviction he cannot see but will not let go: it will go well with those who fear God.
basic.hermeneutics: This passage mixes shrewd counsel with brutal honesty. The advice about the king is practical wisdom, how to survive and flourish near power, not a blank endorsement of every ruler. The hard observations about injustice are description, the Teacher reporting what he sees under the sun, not God prescribing that this is how things should be. The key is to notice where he refuses to stop at appearances. Twice he says a thing is futile, yet between those verses he confesses faith: he knows it will go well with those who fear God. That is the anchor, held by conviction rather than sight.
basic.originalLanguages: Two words carry the passage. Chokmah, wisdom, brightens a face and teaches the right time and procedure, yet cannot master death or fully trace God's work. Hevel, breath or vapor, is the book's refrain, here rendered futile and futility: it names the honoring of the wicked and the scrambling of just deserts, a haze that will not clear on this side of the sun.
basic.typology: The Teacher longs for a judgment that will set right what is crooked, and for a wisdom that can finally comprehend God's work. Both point beyond the book. The unshaken hope that it will go well with those who fear God waits for the resurrection and the last judgment. And the wisdom no man under the sun can find is revealed at last in Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.
basic.christ: The Teacher's ache, that the wicked are honored and the righteous suffer, is answered at the cross, where the only truly Righteous One received what the wicked deserved, and then in the resurrection that vindicated Him. The frustrated hope that a final court will make things right is fulfilled in Christ, appointed by God to judge the living and the dead. The wisdom no one under the sun can grasp is the wisdom of God made known in Him.
basic.god: God is real, present, and to be feared, and He holds the deeds of the wicked and the righteous in His hands. He does not always act on the timetable we would choose, and He does not lay His whole plan open to our inspection. Yet the Teacher trusts His justice: the fear of God is not wasted, and in the end it will go well with those who revere Him.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 13 echoes the call to live rightly under governing authority. Psalm 73 walks the same path, stumbling at the prosperity of the wicked until their end is seen in God's presence. Acts 17 and 2 Timothy 4 announce the judgment the Teacher longs for. Colossians 2 locates all wisdom in Christ.
basic.oneStory: Ecclesiastes 8 stands in the long ache of the Old Testament for a justice that is promised but not yet seen. The Teacher lives honestly in the gap, submitting wisely to authority, refusing to pretend the injustice is not real, and holding by faith that God will finally set it right. The whole story runs on to Christ, in whom the righteous suffer and are vindicated, wisdom is made flesh, and the final judgment is fixed.

context.literary:
Chapter 8 is held together by its frame. It opens with a question about the wise, 'Who is like the wise man? Who knows the interpretation of a matter?', and it closes with a wise man who 'claims to know' and 'is unable to comprehend', verse 17. Between those two verses stand three movements. Verses 1 to 9 are advice about living under a king. Verses 10 to 15 turn to the scandal of the wicked who are honoured, to a confession of faith in verses 12 and 13, and to the contradiction of verse 14. Verses 16 and 17 are a closing reflection on the limits of human understanding. The Teacher moves from the confidence of the sage to the confession of the sage, and so the chapter is a small portrait of his whole book.

The passage is also a conversation between sayings and observations. The first nine verses sound like court wisdom, with commands that could sit in the book of Proverbs: keep the king's command, do not rush from his presence, a wise heart knows the right time. Then the Teacher says 'All this I have seen', verse 9, and the voice shifts to his own observation of what actually happens. The same pattern follows at verse 10, 'Then too, I saw'. The Teacher puts received wisdom beside experience and lets the tension show.

Several words run across the chapter and tie it to the rest of the book. The verb for 'hasten', do not hasten to leave the king's presence, verse 3, is the same verb as 'do not be quick' in 5:2 and 7:9. The language of power in verses 4 and 8 belongs to the same family as the words for God's gift of power in 5:19. The 'time and procedure' of verses 5 and 6 recall the 'time for everything' of chapter 3. And the repeated 'cannot find' of verse 17 returns to 3:11 and 7:24 to 29. The chapter is like a knot in which several of the book's strands are tied.
context.historical:
The first half of the chapter is written in a court setting. In the ancient Near East, the king's word was law, and survival near the throne required a mixture of loyalty and discretion. Proverbs speaks in the same terms: 'The wrath of a king is a messenger of death, but a wise man will pacify it', Proverbs 16:14, and 'When a king's face brightens, there is life', Proverbs 16:15. That is the idea behind the 'brightened face' of verse 1 and the 'stern' face that is changed. Nehemiah, the king's cupbearer, is a good example of a man who knew how to approach a king with wisdom and prayer, Nehemiah 1:11 and 2:1 to 6.

The 'oath before God' in verse 2 has a particular history. In the ancient world a vassal swore an oath of allegiance to the overlord by his gods. Israel's own story shows how this worked. Zedekiah was made to swear by God by Nebuchadnezzar, and the Chronicler counts his rebellion as a sin against that oath, 2 Chronicles 36:13. That gives a possible background to the Teacher's advice to keep the king's command, since the people were bound before God by a sworn loyalty. Other readers take the phrase to refer to the sacred oath by which a servant swore his obedience at the accession of the king.

The word for a 'sentence' in verse 11, pitgam, is a loanword known from the language of royal decrees, and it appears in Esther 1:20 for the king's edict. It suggests an administrative setting in which a verdict had to be carried out by officials, and in which delay was the cause of a general loosening of conscience. Anyone who has seen a system in which crimes are not prosecuted knows what the Teacher means.

The mention of the wicked who 'used to go in and out of the holy place' and were praised in the city points to a religious establishment which a person could use for social standing. The prophets had complained about the same thing, a people who came to the temple and then did evil, Jeremiah 7:9 to 11. The Teacher's observation was not a hypothetical.
context.canonical:
Chapter 8 brings together two lines of Scripture that often seem to pull apart: the call to honour authority and the problem of why God allows the wicked to flourish. On authority, the Old Testament teaches that rulers are to be respected, 'You must not blaspheme God or curse the ruler of your people', Exodus 22:28, and Proverbs adds 'fear the LORD and the king', Proverbs 24:21. The prophets and the apostles hold that this loyalty has a limit: Daniel's friends said that even if God did not deliver them, they would not worship the king's statue, Daniel 3:16 to 18, and Peter said 'We must obey God rather than men', Acts 5:29. The New Testament takes up the Teacher's counsel in Romans 13:1 to 4, which says the authorities that exist have been appointed by God, and in 1 Peter 2:13 to 17, which tells believers to honour the king and fear God. Paul asks for prayers 'for kings and all those in authority', 1 Timothy 2:1 to 2.

On the prosperity of the wicked, the Teacher stands in a long line. Asaph stumbled when he saw it, 'When I tried to understand all this, it was troublesome in my sight until I entered God's sanctuary; then I discerned their end', Psalm 73:16 to 17. Psalm 37 says not to fret over those who do evil, since they wither quickly like grass, Psalm 37:1 to 2. Jeremiah complains and Habakkuk asks why God is silent. Malachi quotes the people saying that it is futile to serve God, and records the answer, that a scroll of remembrance was written for those who feared the LORD, Malachi 3:14 to 18.

The passage also looks forward to the judgment of God. The Teacher says that no one has power over the day of death and that wickedness will not release those who practice it. Paul, speaking to the Athenians, says God 'has set a day when He will judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed', Acts 17:31. Timothy is charged in the presence of Christ Jesus, 'who will judge the living and the dead', 2 Timothy 4:1. And the cry of the martyrs, 'How long, O Lord?', Revelation 6:10, is the same cry that the Teacher cannot answer.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The Teacher wants his hearers to live well in a world they do not control. The first half of the chapter is practical advice to subjects of a king: keep your word, do not leave the royal presence in a temper, do not make a stand on a bad cause, and learn the right time and manner for each thing. He is not asking for servility. He is saying that a wise person knows when to speak and when to wait, because the one who holds power 'will do whatever he pleases' and the cost of misjudging it falls on the subject. Anyone who has worked under an authority they did not choose will see the value in that.

He also wants them to know that the system does not close the question of justice. Power can seem to settle everything, and for the one under it, everything does seem settled. The Teacher keeps the question open by pointing to what no ruler controls: the day of death, the wind, the future. Even the most powerful person is a man under a higher authority, and the chapter is arranged so that the reader sees it.

Then he wants them to hold on to two things at once that most people hold separately. The first is that the Teacher has seen injustice and does not pretend it away. The second is that he knows it will go well with those who fear God. He does not reconcile these in a theory. He means his hearers to live in the gap, practising their faith in the fear of God without pretending to have the explanation, and to be glad in the ordinary gifts of eating and drinking as they wait. The last verses are meant to humble the clever, since no one, however wise, can map out the work of God.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The first half of the chapter is advice, and the second half is largely report. The Teacher tells subjects how to behave near a king, in the tone of a seasoned court official, and these are principles of prudence, not a doctrine of absolute obedience. He does not say that the king is always right. He says the king can do what he pleases and that an unwise person will suffer for provoking him. The distinction matters, because a reader who takes verses 2 to 5 as an unqualified command to obey every ruler would be forced to say the same of rulers who commanded evil. The rest of Scripture does not allow that: the midwives of Exodus 1 disobeyed Pharaoh, Daniel kept praying, and the apostles said 'We must obey God rather than men', Acts 5:29. The Teacher's counsel is for ordinary dealings with ordinary authority, and not a charter for tyranny.

The observations in verses 10 to 14 are what the Teacher sees: the wicked buried with honour, the delay of sentences, the righteous and wicked exchanging their rewards. He does not call any of that good and does not tell us to accept it. He calls it futile, which is the book's word for what is distorted and cannot be grasped. Believers should respond to the same sights with justice where they can act and with prayer where they cannot.

The verse that functions as a command is verse 15, to eat, drink and be glad, and it is better seen as his considered counsel on what to do in the meantime. It does not mean that nothing else is required, since the book will end with the call to fear God and keep His commandments. It means that the joy of ordinary gifts is part of faithful living, even in a world where much is unresolved.

debates.question: What is the 'oath before God' in verse 2?

views.label: A loyalty oath sworn to the king in God's name
views.case: In the ancient world a subject or vassal swore allegiance in the name of the deity. Zedekiah swore by God to Nebuchadnezzar and was condemned for rebelling against it, 2 Chronicles 36:13. On this reading the Teacher's advice rests on the sacredness of that oath, and keeping the king's command is a way of keeping one's word to God.

views.label: An oath of obedience to God Himself
views.case: The phrase can be read 'because of the oath of God', that is, the commitment that a person has made to God. In that case, the teacher is recalling the vows in 5:4 to 5, which warn that God has no pleasure in fools and that vows must be paid. Obedience to the king would be a way of respecting the vows made before God.

views.label: A general reference to the God appointed order
views.case: Some take it as a looser phrase for the duty that arises from God's own authority over rulers, the sort of idea Paul develops in Romans 13:1, that the authorities have been appointed by God. On this reading no specific oath is in view.

debates.bearing: The Hebrew is compact enough to allow more than one reading, and the practical point is the same in each: the Teacher grounds submission in a person's relation to God, and not in fear of the king alone. That also sets the limit, because a duty rooted in God cannot require disobedience to Him.

debates.question: Are verses 12 and 13 the Teacher's own conviction, or a conventional saying that he is about to qualify?

views.label: They express his settled faith
views.case: The verses open with 'I also know', which marks a conviction held against the evidence. They fit the book's closing conclusion, 'Fear God and keep His commandments', 12:13, and the statement that God will bring every deed into judgment, 12:14. On this reading verses 12 and 13 are the anchor of the chapter.

views.label: They quote the traditional teaching, which verse 14 then tests
views.case: Some read the verses as a quotation of the orthodox claim that the God fearing prosper and the wicked do not, which the Teacher sets beside the experience of verse 14, where the righteous suffer what the wicked deserve. The tension then becomes the point, a protest against over simple retribution.

views.label: They look beyond the present life
views.case: Others read the verse as the Teacher's confidence in an ultimate verdict, not an observation about what happens in this life. It will go well with those who fear God, even if the evidence is not seen under the sun. This reading finds support in the book's judgment passages, 3:17 and 12:14, and in the New Testament's account of the final judgment.

debates.bearing: The passage can hold more than one of these at once. The Teacher plainly believes what he says in verse 12 and plainly sees what he says in verse 14. The tension is not a contradiction but the shape of faith in a fallen world: God's justice is trusted when it is not yet seen.

debates.question: Was the wicked 'praised' or 'forgotten' in verse 10?

views.label: They were praised in the city
views.case: The BSB follows some Hebrew manuscripts, the Septuagint and the Vulgate, and reads that the wicked were praised in the city where they had done so. It fits the grievance: the people who used the holy place for show were honoured at their funerals.

views.label: They were soon forgotten
views.case: Most Hebrew manuscripts read 'were soon forgotten', as the BSB footnote notes. The sting then lies elsewhere: the wicked came and went from the holy place and were buried with ceremony, but their memory soon fades. This sits well with the theme that no one's name endures.

debates.bearing: Both readings underline the same scandal, that the wicked had a religious standing and an honoured burial. Whichever is right, the Teacher calls it futile, and the question of final justice is left to God.

study.originalLanguages:
The word that binds the first half of the chapter is shilton, 'supreme', in 'the king's word is supreme' in verse 4, and the related verb in verse 8, where no one has 'authority' over the day of death, and in verse 9, where one man 'lords it over' another. It is the same family of words as in 5:19, where God gives the power to enjoy, and in 6:2, where He does not allow it. The Teacher is tracing a theme: real power, in the end, is not in the king's hand but in God's. The language that is applied to the king in verse 4 is a humble echo of the language used of God elsewhere. 'He will do whatever he pleases' in verse 3 uses the phrase that the Psalms use of the LORD: 'He does as He pleases', Psalm 115:3. And the question 'Who can say to him, "What are you doing?"' has its pattern in Job 9:12 and Daniel 4:35, where it is God who cannot be questioned. The Teacher uses the language of divine sovereignty for a king, and then shows in verses 8 to 13 that the king is not the one with the last word.

The verb in verse 3, 'hasten', is the same as in 5:2, 'do not be hasty in your heart to utter a word before God', and in 7:9, 'do not be quickly provoked'. It appears three times in a handful of chapters, and each time it recommends patience. A person who is quick in speech before God, quick to anger and quick to leave an authority in a temper has the same fault. The verb makes a thread of the book's counsel on slowing down.

The phrase 'time and procedure' in verses 5 and 6 pairs the word for time with the word mishpat, which also means justice or judgment. A wise heart knows the right time and the right judgment, and the double meaning of mishpat is helpful. It means procedure, how things are done properly, and it means justice, what is right. The Teacher hints that the same wise heart that knows how to approach a king also knows that a day of judgment is coming, which is what the book says in 3:17 and 12:14.

The word for 'interpretation' in verse 1, pesher, is a rare noun. It is the word that later Jewish interpreters would use for their method of explaining a prophecy, and the Teacher uses it for the explanation of a matter. His question 'Who knows?' hints that such an explanation is exactly what is in short supply.

The phrase 'it will go well' in verses 12 and 13 is the Hebrew for 'it will be good', and the Teacher sets it against 'the days will not lengthen like a shadow', literally like the shade of the late afternoon. The shadow image links this chapter with 6:12 and 7:12. A life that is lived without the fear of God is a shadow that does not grow, and it fades with the light.

Finally, in verse 15 the Teacher 'commended' joy. The verb is the one used in 4:2 when he 'admired' the dead. In the one place he praises the dead, in the other he praises joy. And the statement that joy will 'accompany' a man in his labour uses a verb that means to join or attend. Where 5:15 says that a man takes nothing in his hand, 8:15 says that joy goes with him. It is the one companion of toil.

typology.type: The king whose word is supreme, 8:2 to 4
typology.fulfillment: The Teacher says that the king's word is supreme and that no one can ask him 'What are you doing?' The prophets speak of a king whose reign will be one of justice, Isaiah 9:6 to 7, and Jesus claims all authority in heaven and on earth, Matthew 28:18. The earthly king's absolute word is a faint echo of the word of the Lord, who is 'upholding all things by His powerful word', Hebrews 1:3. The correspondence breaks at a key point: the human king cannot be questioned because he is unaccountable, while Christ cannot be questioned because He is always just. The type falls short because the earthly king is himself under judgment.

typology.type: The righteous who receive what the wicked deserve, 8:14
typology.fulfillment: The Teacher sees that righteous men sometimes get what the wicked deserve. The cross is where this reaches its limit and is turned into good. Christ, who knew no sin, was made sin for us, 2 Corinthians 5:21, and bore our sins in His body on the tree, 1 Peter 2:24. And the exchange also runs in the other direction: those who deserved wrath received righteousness. The type is fulfilled in a reversal that the Teacher could not have expected: it is for others' sake that the righteous One suffered.

typology.type: The longing for a verdict that will make the difference clear
typology.fulfillment: The Teacher says that the wicked will not escape and that it will go well with those who fear God, though he cannot see it. Paul says that God has appointed a day to judge the world by a Man, and has given proof by raising Him, Acts 17:31. In Christ the longing has a name, and the judge is the one who died for His people, Romans 8:34. The scene of Revelation 20:11 to 15 is the final fulfilment. The type falls short because the Teacher expresses a hope, while the gospel grounds it in an event.

typology.type: The wisdom that no man can comprehend, 8:16 to 17
typology.fulfillment: The Teacher says that no one can comprehend the work of God, however hard he searches. Christ is called the wisdom of God, 1 Corinthians 1:24, and in Him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, Colossians 2:3. He says, 'No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him', Matthew 11:27. The correspondence is that what could not be searched out is revealed. The type is still partial, since even revealed wisdom is known in part now, 1 Corinthians 13:12.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ through its two great frustrations: the injustice that is not corrected and the wisdom that cannot be found. Both are met in Him, and the way they are met is not what the Teacher could have guessed.

On injustice, the chapter's sharpest line is that there are 'righteous men who get what the actions of the wicked deserve'. That is the story of the cross. The only wholly righteous man who has ever lived was condemned by a court, handed over by a religious establishment, and executed under a governor who knew he was innocent. Isaiah said, 'He was assigned a grave with the wicked', Isaiah 53:9. The gospel does not argue that this was fair. It says that it was the way God dealt with the problem the Teacher cannot solve. who 'bore our sins in His body on the tree', 1 Peter 2:24, so that the unrighteous might be given what the righteous One deserved, and the righteous One what the unrighteous deserved, in the reverse of verse 14, and by choice.

It also shows how Christ lived under authority. The Teacher advises a wise submission to the king, and Jesus showed it, though in His own way. He paid the temple tax so as not to give offence, Matthew 17:24 to 27, He said to give to Caesar what is Caesar's, Matthew 22:21, and He told Pilate 'You would have no authority over Me if it were not given you from above', John 19:11. That last statement is the nearest New Testament mirror to the Teacher's insight that rulers are under a higher power. And He did not use that knowledge to escape. He submitted, in the knowledge that His Father was supreme.

On the future, the Teacher says that no one knows what will happen. Jesus does. He has told His disciples about the judgment, and He has been raised as the sign of it. Paul declares that God 'has set a day when He will judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed. He has given proof of this to everyone by raising Him from the dead', Acts 17:31. The 'it will go well with those who fear God' of verse 12 is no longer only a conviction. It is held by the Christian on the ground that Jesus has risen. The hope that was invisible to the Teacher is now visible in the empty tomb.

And on wisdom, the Teacher says that no one can comprehend the work of God. Christ is the wisdom of God and in Him are all the treasures of wisdom, 1 Corinthians 1:24 and Colossians 2:3. He says that He reveals the Father, Matthew 11:27. The more one knows of Him, the more the 'cannot find' of verse 17 gives way to 'have found', and to a wisdom that is ready to say, with Paul, that we know in part and will one day know fully, 1 Corinthians 13:12.

A note of caution should be kept. The Teacher is not describing Jesus, and the king of verse 2 is not a type of Christ. The connections are those made by the New Testament, where Christ stands at the place of the cross, the judgment and the wisdom.
study.god:
The Teacher's God is above kings. The first half of the chapter has a king whose word is supreme, but the repeated reminders of what no ruler can do, such as controlling the wind, avoiding death or knowing the future, show that he too is a creature. Behind the king there is another authority, and the instruction in verse 2 to keep the king's command 'because of your oath before God' puts God as the ground of all earthly order. This is what Paul says in Romans 13:1, 'there is no authority except that which is from God', and it keeps the Christian from both of the two errors, worshipping the state and despising it.

He is also a God who is to be feared. The phrase 'those who fear God' appears three times in two verses, and it describes people who are 'reverent in His presence', verse 12. The fear is the Teacher's whole answer to the puzzle of the chapter. It is not a technique for getting results, because the Teacher has just said that results are not guaranteed. It is an orientation toward a God whose holiness and goodness are real whether or not we can see them operating.

There is also a patient God. Verse 11 says that when a sentence is not carried out quickly, human hearts are encouraged in evil. The Bible reads the same delay in two ways. It can be a sign of human negligence, as it is when an official fails to act. It can also be a sign of divine patience, as Peter says, 'The Lord is not slow in keeping His promise as some understand slowness, but is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish', 2 Peter 3:9, and Paul says that God's kindness leads to repentance, Romans 2:4 to 5. Ezekiel records God asking, 'Do I take any pleasure in the death of the wicked?', Ezekiel 18:23. The Teacher does not interpret the delay, and the doctrine of God in the whole Bible is that mercy is one of its meanings.

God is also inscrutable. 'Even if the wise man claims to know, he is unable to comprehend.' The Bible holds that God has made Himself known, and it also holds that His ways are higher than ours. Paul's exclamation in Romans 11:33 is the right commentary: 'How unsearchable are His judgments, and untraceable His ways!' This humbles every theory that claims to explain why a particular person suffers, as the friends of Job learned. And it keeps worship from becoming a bargain, since God is not a machine of reward.

Finally, God is the giver of joy. In the middle of the argument the Teacher stops to say that he commends enjoyment, 'because there is nothing better for a man under the sun than to eat and drink and be merry', verse 15. That statement shows a generous God, who has given gifts to be enjoyed even in a world where He has not yet put everything right. In worship, this teaches us to give thanks for the ordinary and to bring our unanswered questions without pretending they are answered. It teaches us to pray, with the martyrs, 'How long, O Lord?', Revelation 6:10, and to trust the One who will answer.

crossReferences.note: Paul says that everyone must submit to the governing authorities because there is no authority except from God. It is the New Testament parallel to Ecclesiastes 8:2 to 5, with the same ground, that submission is owed because of God, and with the same limit, since authority is God's servant for good.

Peter tells believers to submit to every human institution for the Lord's sake, to honour the king and to fear God. The two commands stand side by side, as in Ecclesiastes 8:2 and 8:12 to 13, where respect for the king is held together with the fear of God.

When the authorities forbade the apostles to preach, Peter said they must obey God rather than men. It marks the boundary of Ecclesiastes 8:2 to 4: the Teacher teaches prudence near power, and the apostles show that the king's word is not supreme over God's.

A king's wrath is a messenger of death, but a wise man will pacify it, and a king's bright face means life. It is the background of Ecclesiastes 8:1 to 4, with the brightened face and the stern one, and it shows the Teacher using the court wisdom of Proverbs.

Asaph was troubled by the prosperity of the wicked until he entered God's sanctuary and discerned their end. It parallels Ecclesiastes 8:10 to 14, where the wicked go in and out of the holy place, and it offers a resolution in God's presence which the Teacher can only hope for.

The people say that it is futile to serve God and that the arrogant are blessed. The LORD answers that a scroll of remembrance was written for those who fear Him, and that they will again see the difference between the righteous and the wicked. It is the same complaint as Ecclesiastes 8:14, and the same answer as 8:12.

Job says of God, 'Who dares to ask Him, What are You doing?' The Teacher asks the same question of the king in Ecclesiastes 8:4. The echo suggests that the king's power is a borrowed version of what belongs to God, and it prepares the move from king to God in 8:12.

The psalmist says not to fret over those who do evil, for they wither quickly like grass. It matches the Teacher's statement in Ecclesiastes 8:13 that the wicked's days will not lengthen like a shadow, and it gives the same counsel, to trust in the LORD and wait.

Paul says God has set a day when He will judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed, and has given proof by raising Him. It supplies the evidence that the Teacher lacks when he says in Ecclesiastes 8:12 that it will go well with those who fear God.

The Teacher says God has made everything beautiful in its time and has set eternity in human hearts, yet no one can fathom His work from beginning to end. Ecclesiastes 8:17 returns to the same limit, now with the added cost of sleepless effort.

The conclusion of the book says to fear God and keep His commandments, because God will bring every deed into judgment. It is the full statement of what Ecclesiastes 8:12 to 13 expresses as a conviction held in the middle of puzzlement.

The souls under the altar cry out, 'How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You avenge our blood?' It is the voice of Ecclesiastes 8:11 and 8:14 given a heavenly setting, and it shows the delay of justice as a matter on which the whole Bible waits for God's answer.

study.oneStory:
Ecclesiastes 8 belongs to the long stretch of the Bible between a promise and its keeping. The story begins with a world under God's good rule, and the first rebellion, Genesis 3, introduces two things that the chapter describes: human rulers who lord it over one another to their own harm, and a world in which the verdict is delayed. God's first response to the fall is not an immediate sentence of the full penalty. The sentence is given, but the offender is clothed and sent out, and life goes on. The delay of verse 11 begins there, as a mixture of mercy and testing.

From there the story is about kingdoms. Israel asked for a king like the nations, 1 Samuel 8, and was warned what a king would take. Some kings did what was right, many did not, and the prophets pronounced judgment on those who used their power to crush the poor. The Teacher's advice to be wise near a king is made in the middle of this history. The exile that followed put God's people under foreign kings, and Daniel's story shows what faith looks like in that setting: honour the ruler, refuse to worship him, and trust that that the Most High rules over the kingdom of mankind, Daniel 4:32. That statement is the answer to the question the Teacher is asking about where the final authority lies.

The prophets and the psalmists took up the other question, the prosperity of the wicked. They answered it with a promise: God will judge. Habakkuk is told that the righteous will live by faith, Habakkuk 2:4, which is the Teacher's 'it will go well with those who fear God' in a prophetic form. The New Testament adds the substance. Jesus is the righteous sufferer who was vindicated, and He is the appointed judge, Acts 17:31. The church lives between His first coming and His second, with the Teacher's ache and the martyrs' cry, 'How long?', Revelation 6:10, and with the assurance that the answer has been given in the resurrection.

The story ends with the verdict. In Revelation, the dead are judged according to their deeds, and the unrighteous are no longer honoured, Revelation 20:11 to 15. The kingdoms of the world become the kingdom of the Lord and of His Christ, Revelation 11:15, and the one who sits on the throne wipes away every tear, Revelation 21:4. The Teacher's confession that no one can comprehend the work of God is met by a world in which 'they will see His face', Revelation 22:4, and where knowing in part gives way to knowing fully. The injustice he could only report is finally put right, and the joy that he could only commend in small amounts becomes the whole of life.

quiz.q: What counsel does the Teacher give about living under a king?

options.text: Keep the king's command wisely, honoring your oath before God, while discerning the right time and manner.
options.note: He teaches prudent, reverent submission that still weighs the right time and procedure.

options.text: Obey the king in absolutely everything without any thought of God.
options.note: He urges real submission, but always as one answerable to God, not the king alone.

options.text: Ignore rulers, since their word means nothing.
options.note: The opposite of the text; the king's word is supreme and is to be taken seriously.

options.text: Overthrow any ruler who displeases you.
options.note: The Teacher counsels wise navigation, not rebellion.

quiz.q: What is the anchor conviction the Teacher holds in the middle of the injustice?

options.text: That it will go well with those who fear God, and not with the wicked.
options.note: This is the faith he confesses between his two verdicts of futility.

options.text: That the wicked will always be punished immediately in this life.
options.note: He says the opposite; sentences often go unexecuted and the wicked live long.

options.text: That God does not really care about justice at all.
options.note: He trusts God's justice; that trust is the point of the passage.

options.text: That fearing God brings a reverent life whose end is secure in God's hands.
options.note: True and close, though the sharp claim is that it will go well with those who fear Him.

quiz.q: What does the Teacher mean by calling things futile in this chapter?

options.text: Hevel, a breath or vapor, names what he cannot grasp: the wicked honored and just deserts reversed.
options.note: Hevel is the book's keyword for the ungraspable haze over life under the sun.

options.text: That everything is worthless and nothing matters.
options.note: Hevel is not flat nihilism; he still commends joy and fears God.

options.text: That life is fleeting and hard to pin down, so injustice galls all the more.
options.note: A fair sense of the word, though here it targets the specific scandal of injustice.

options.text: That God has made a mistake in running the world.
options.note: He never charges God with error; he trusts God even where he cannot see.

quiz.q: What does the Teacher conclude about understanding God's work?

options.text: No one under the sun can fully comprehend it, not even the wise who claim to.
options.note: He confesses the real limit of human wisdom before God's ways.

options.text: The wise can eventually figure out everything God is doing.
options.note: He says the opposite; even the wise cannot find it out.

options.text: God's work is largely beyond us, so we should trust rather than pretend to master it.
options.note: The right response, though the verse stresses the sheer limit of comprehension.

options.text: Only kings can understand what God is doing.
options.note: Nothing in the text grants rulers such insight; the limit falls on all.

quiz.q: How does this chapter point forward to Christ?

options.text: The Righteous One receiving what the wicked deserve, the longed for judgment, and hidden wisdom all find their answer in Christ.
options.note: The cross, the coming judgment, and the wisdom of God converge in Jesus.

options.text: It shows Jesus as merely another wise teacher offering good advice.
options.note: It points to far more than advice: to His atoning death, vindication, and judgment.

options.text: It gives detailed rules for royal court etiquette that Jesus later repeats.
options.note: This misses the passage's forward reach to Christ entirely.

options.text: Its ache for justice and for wisdom is met in Christ, who suffered, was vindicated, and will judge.
options.note: True and well put, though the sharpest link is the Righteous One bearing the wicked's due.

questions: The Teacher urges wisdom in knowing the right time and manner for things. Where do you need discernment, not just courage, in how you speak or act under someone else's authority right now?
He looked honestly at injustice and still would not stop fearing God. Where are you tempted to let unfairness you have seen erode your trust in God's justice?
It will go well with those who fear God is a conviction held by faith, not sight. What would it look like to rest on that promise this week when the wicked seem to prosper?
The Teacher admitted that no one can fully comprehend God's work. Where do you need to trade the demand to understand everything for the freedom of trusting God with what you cannot see?
He received food, drink, and joy in labor as gifts from God's hand. What ordinary good gift could you receive today with gratitude rather than let it pass by unnoticed?

translationNotes.note: This too is futile renders hevel, the book's keyword, literally a breath or vapor. It names the honoring of the wicked as something that cannot be made sense of on its own terms.
Futility and futile again translate hevel. The word does not mean worthless so much as ungraspable, a haze; here it targets the reversal of just deserts between the righteous and the wicked.

Under the sun is the Teacher's recurring phrase for life viewed within this world's horizon. It frames both the injustice he sees and the wisdom he cannot find, until the horizon of God's judgment and God's wisdom breaks in.
